noteBlocks.lede: In a right-angled triangle, fix one angle and the ratios between the sides are fixed too. That is all sine, cosine and tangent are: three ratios that depend on the angle alone. They are how a surveyor gets the height of a building from a tape measure and one angle, without leaving the ground.

Choose sine, cosine or tangent from the two sides involved.
Rearrange the ratio before substituting, and round only at the end.

noteBlocks.md: Three ratios, one labelling routine, and a rearrangement. Stand at the angle you are working with, name the three sides, and the two the question mentions choose the ratio for you. The marks are lost not on the ratio itself but on labelling, on rearranging, and on rounding too early.

noteBlocks.caption: Move to the other acute angle and opposite and adjacent swap over. Only the hypotenuse stays where it is.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which side of a right-angled triangle is the hypotenuse?
noteBlocks.answer: The side opposite the right angle
noteBlocks.explain: Yes, and it is always the longest side. It is the one label that never changes when you move to the other angle.
options: The side opposite the right angle
The side next to the angle you are using

noteBlocks.md:
Stand at the angle you are working with and name the three sides:

**Hypotenuse** — opposite the right angle, always.
**Opposite** — the side facing your angle across the triangle.
**Adjacent** — the remaining side, beside your angle.

Then the two sides in play choose the ratio for you:

$\sin\theta = \dfrac{O}{H} \qquad \cos\theta = \dfrac{A}{H} \qquad \tan\theta = \dfrac{O}{A}$

noteBlocks.prompt: You know the hypotenuse and want the side opposite the angle. Which ratio?

noteBlocks.title: Not on the formula sheet
noteBlocks.md:
The Higher sheet prints the **sine rule**, the **cosine rule** and $\tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ — all for triangles with **no** right angle.
SOH CAH TOA is not printed anywhere, so it has to be known. If a triangle has a right angle marked, these three ratios are the tools, not the rules on the sheet.

noteBlocks.prompt: A triangle has a right angle marked. Which tools apply?
noteBlocks.explain: The rules on the formula sheet are for triangles with no right angle, so a right angle means these three ratios.

noteBlocks.text: Rearranging: is the unknown on the top or the bottom?

noteBlocks.md:
Write the ratio as an **equation** before you touch the calculator. Then look at where the unknown sits.

**On top** — as in $\sin 38° = \dfrac{x}{9.4}$ — multiply: $x = 9.4\sin 38°$.
**On the bottom** — as in $\cos 54° = \dfrac{8.5}{y}$ — divide: $y = \dfrac{8.5}{\cos 54°}$.

A quick sense check catches most slips: the hypotenuse must come out **longer** than either short side.

noteBlocks.explain: Yes: $y = 8.5 \div \cos 54° = 14.4611$, so 14.5 cm. Multiplying instead would have given 5.0, shorter than the side you started with.

noteBlocks.title: November 2025, M3 Q24
noteBlocks.md:
A routine side by cosine. **Under a fifth** of candidates got all three marks: cosine was identified but not rearranged, and many assumed a different side was wanted and reached for tangent.
The fix is mechanical: label O, A and H on the diagram, write the equation, then rearrange.

noteBlocks.title: Trigonometry: Missing Angles
noteBlocks.why: Five minutes on going the other way: two sides in, an angle out. Watch the inverse key being used at the end of every example.

noteBlocks.prompt: $\tan\theta = \dfrac{4.2}{7.5}$. Find $\theta$ in degrees, to 1 decimal place.
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: the ratio is 0.5600, and $\tan^{-1}(0.5600) = 29.2°$. The ratio on its own is not the angle.

noteBlocks.md:
Both angles are measured from the **horizontal**.

**Elevation** is how far you look up; **depression** is how far you look down. An angle of depression from a cliff top equals the angle of elevation from the boat below, because the two horizontals are parallel.

Watch where the triangle starts. If a question gives someone's **eye height**, the triangle sits on that line, so the eye height is added at the end — in the same unit.

noteBlocks.alt: A right-angled triangle for an angle of elevation of 32 degrees from a point 45 m away, with the height above eye level marked h.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='tg24'><title id='tg24'>An angle of elevation of 32 degrees from a point 45 m away</title><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.7'><path d='M54,196 L250,196 L250,73.5 Z'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2'><path d='M237,196 V183 H250'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2'><path d='M88,196 A34,34 0 0 0 82.8,178'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1' stroke-dasharray='5 4'><path d='M54,196 H280'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit' font-size='13'><text x='94' y='184'>32°</text><text x='152' y='216' text-anchor='middle'>45 m</text><text x='260' y='134.8'>h m</text><text x='152' y='234' text-anchor='middle'>horizontal at eye level</text></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit' font-size='11'><text x='6' y='16'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='6' y='29'>accurately</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: $h = 45\tan 32° = 28.12$ m above eye level, so the tree is $28.12 + 1.6 = 29.7$ m tall.

noteBlocks.prompt: Trigonometry gives 28.12 m above eye level, and the eyes are 160 cm above the ground. What is the full height in metres, to 1 decimal place?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: 160 cm is 1.6 m, and 28.12 + 1.6 = 29.72, so 29.7 m. Adding 160 as metres would have given a tree over a hundred metres tall.

noteBlocks.md:
An isosceles triangle has no right angle, but dropping a **perpendicular from the apex to the base** creates two right-angled triangles. The base is halved; the equal sides are not. The ratio then gives **half** the angle at the top, so double it.

When one triangle feeds another, carry the **unrounded** value across. Rounding in the middle is the single most reliable way to lose the final accuracy mark.

noteBlocks.alt: An isosceles triangle of base 2.6 m and equal sides 3.4 m, split by a dashed perpendicular into two right-angled triangles with bases of 1.3 m.
noteBlocks.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 258' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='tg25'><title id='tg25'>An isosceles triangle split by a perpendicular into two right-angled triangles</title><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.7'><path d='M56,200 L264,200 L160,56 Z'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.1' stroke-dasharray='5 4'><path d='M160,56 L160,200'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2'><path d='M147,200 V187 H160'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit' font-size='13'><text x='108' y='222' text-anchor='middle'>1.3 m</text><text x='212' y='222' text-anchor='middle'>1.3 m</text><text x='90' y='128'>3.4 m</text><text x='200' y='128'>3.4 m</text><text x='160' y='242' text-anchor='middle'>2.6 m</text><text x='160' y='96' text-anchor='middle'>apex</text></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='inherit' font-size='11'><text x='6' y='16'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='6' y='29'>accurately</text></g></svg>
noteBlocks.caption: Half the base is 1.3 m, so $\sin(\text{half angle}) = 1.3 \div 3.4$, the half angle is $22.5°$ and the apex angle is $45.0°$.

noteBlocks.prompt: An isosceles triangle has base 2.6 m and equal sides 3.4 m. What length goes into the ratio as the base of the right-angled triangle, in metres?
noteBlocks.explain: Yes: the perpendicular halves the base, so 2.6 ÷ 2 = 1.3 m. Using the whole base scored zero in Summer 2024.

noteBlocks.title: Why size does not matter
noteBlocks.md: Two right-angled triangles with the same acute angle are one shape at two scales, so each side of one is the same multiple of the matching side. Dividing one side by another cancels that multiple, so $\sin\theta$ depends on the angle alone.

noteBlocks.explain: Yes. The sides all double, so the ratio between any two of them is unchanged. That is why a single angle fixes all three ratios.

noteBlocks.md:
Label the three sides from the angle in use.
Choose sine, cosine or tangent from the two sides.
Rearrange first, and round once at the end.

Three marks for a single side or angle, four when something has to be added at the end. The first mark is the ratio written as an equation with the right sides in it; the second the rearrangement or the inverse; the last the value rounded as asked, with its unit or degree sign. Stuck: label the triangle and write any correct ratio you can see — a correct equation earns the method mark.

workedExamples.stem:
The diagram shows a right-angled triangle. The hypotenuse is 9.4 m and one angle is 38°.

Calculate the length of the side labelled $x$. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

steps.working: from the 38° angle: $x$ is **opposite**, 9.4 m is the **hypotenuse**
steps.decision: Label the triangle from the angle you are given, every time. The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle; opposite and adjacent then depend on which angle you are standing at.

options: Because opposite and adjacent are named from the angle you are working with
Because the longest side is always opposite
whyMenu.explain: Move to the other acute angle and opposite and adjacent swap over. Only the hypotenuse stays put.

steps.decision: SOH: sine uses Opposite over Hypotenuse. Writing the equation before rearranging is the method mark, and it is the line the November 2025 report says candidates could not produce.
The unknown is on the top, so multiply. Keep the full display: if this length is used again later, rounding now would cost the accuracy mark.
Round once, at the end, exactly as the question asks. Check it is sensible: the opposite side must be shorter than the hypotenuse, and it is.

steps.working: from the 54° angle: 8.5 cm is **adjacent**, $y$ is the **hypotenuse**
steps.decision: Label first. Adjacent and hypotenuse are the two sides in play, so the ratio is cosine.
CAH: cosine is Adjacent over Hypotenuse. This time the unknown is on the bottom, which changes what happens next.

options: Because the unknown is the denominator, so you divide rather than multiply
Because the hypotenuse is always the answer
whyMenu.explain: Multiply both sides by y, then divide by cos 54°. The unknown ends up as 8.5 ÷ cos 54°, not 8.5 × cos 54°.

A right-angled triangle has the side opposite an angle $\theta$ equal to 4.2 cm, and the side adjacent to it equal to 7.5 cm.

Calculate the size of angle $\theta$. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

steps.working: opposite $= 4.2$, adjacent $= 7.5$, so the ratio is tangent
steps.decision: Two sides are known and an angle is wanted, so this is an inverse trigonometry question, not Pythagoras. Pythagoras would give the third side, which is not what was asked.

options: Because an angle is wanted, and Pythagoras only ever gives lengths
Because there are two sides given
whyMenu.explain: The November 2024 report noted candidates using Pythagoras to find a third side when the question asked for an angle.

steps.decision: TOA: tangent is Opposite over Adjacent. Write the ratio down before touching the calculator.
The inverse key undoes the ratio and returns the angle. On a calculator that is shift then tan; make sure the calculator is in degrees.
Sense check: the opposite side is shorter than the adjacent side, so the angle should be less than 45°, and 29.2° is.

Ciara stands 45 m from the foot of a tree, on level ground. Her eyes are 160 cm above the ground. The angle of elevation of the top of the tree from her eyes is 32°.

Calculate the height of the tree. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

figure.alt: A right-angled triangle showing a line of sight rising at 32 degrees from eye level. The horizontal distance is 45 m and the height of the tree above eye level is marked h m.

steps.working: draw the triangle from the eyes, not from the ground
steps.decision: The angle of elevation is measured from the horizontal at eye level, so the triangle sits on a line 1.6 m above the ground. Whatever the triangle gives has that 1.6 m added at the end.

options: Because the angle is measured from the horizontal line through her eyes
Because her height does not matter
Because the tree grows from eye level
whyMenu.explain: The line of sight starts at her eyes. The triangle therefore gives only the part of the tree above eye level.

steps.decision: Convert before you add. The Summer 2023 report traced a common wrong answer to a height in centimetres being added to a length in metres.
Opposite and adjacent, so tangent. Keep every figure on the display; this value is about to be added to something.
Add the eye height last and round once. Rounding $28.11912$ to $28.1$ before adding would give $29.70$, and the accuracy mark would be at risk.

parts.stem:
A cliff is 45 m high. A boat is 120 m from the foot of the cliff.

Calculate the angle of depression of the boat from the top of the cliff. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: tan t = 45 / 120 (angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from the boat)

hints: The angle of depression is measured from the horizontal at the top, not from the cliff face.
It is equal to the angle of elevation from the boat, because the two horizontals are parallel.
parts.workedSolution: The horizontal at the cliff top is parallel to the sea, so the angle of depression equals the angle of elevation from the boat. $\tan \theta = \dfrac{45}{120} = 0.3750$, so $\theta = 20.5560°$, which is $20.6°$.

commonErrors.feedback: That angle is measured from the cliff face rather than from the horizontal. Depression and elevation both start at a horizontal line.
That is the distance from the cliff top to the boat, found by Pythagoras. The question asks for an angle.

parts.stem:
A pair of step ladders makes an isosceles triangle. Each side is 3.4 m long and the feet are 2.6 m apart.

Calculate the angle at the top between the two sides. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: Drop a perpendicular from the top to the middle of the base.
That creates two right-angled triangles, each with a base of half the original.
The ratio gives half the angle at the top, so double it at the end.
parts.workedSolution:
Dropping a perpendicular from the apex splits the triangle into two right-angled triangles, each with a base of $2.6 \div 2 = 1.3$ m and a hypotenuse of 3.4 m.

$\sin(\text{half angle}) = \dfrac{1.3}{3.4} = 0.3824$, so the half angle is $22.4795°$ and the full angle at the top is $2 \times 22.4795 = 44.9590°$, which is $45.0°$.

commonErrors.feedback: The whole base has been used in the ratio. The perpendicular splits it, so the right-angled triangle has a base of 1.3 m.
That is half of the angle at the top, which is what the right-angled triangle gives. Double it for the full angle between the two sides.

parts.stem:
A ladder 4.6 m long leans against a vertical wall. It makes an angle of 71° with the horizontal ground.

Calculate the distance from the foot of the ladder to the wall. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

scheme.examinerNote: 3 marks is the tariff for a single ratio in the M3 papers read (November 2025 Q24, November 2024 Q25)

hints: The ladder is the hypotenuse.
The distance along the ground is adjacent to the 71° angle.
parts.workedSolution: The ladder is the hypotenuse and the distance along the ground is adjacent to the angle, so $\cos 71° = \dfrac{d}{4.6}$ and $d = 4.6\cos 71° = 1.4976$ m, which is $1.5$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: Sine gives the height the ladder reaches up the wall, which is the side opposite the angle. The distance along the ground is adjacent, so use cosine.
Dividing gives a distance longer than the ladder itself. With the unknown on top, multiply.
Tangent has been used with the ladder, but the ladder is the hypotenuse and tangent never involves it. Adjacent with hypotenuse means cosine.

parts.stem:
A ramp is 5.8 m long and rises 0.9 m from the ground to a doorway.

Calculate the angle the ramp makes with the horizontal. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: The ramp is the hypotenuse and the rise is opposite the angle.
Two sides and an angle wanted means an inverse ratio.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the horizontal distance the ramp covers, found by Pythagoras. An angle needs an inverse trigonometric ratio.
That is the sine of the angle. Press the inverse sine to turn the ratio into degrees.
Tangent has been used with the hypotenuse. Tangent needs the two shorter sides; here the ramp is the hypotenuse.

parts.stem:
A guideline says that a ramp of this kind must make an angle of no more than 10° with the horizontal.

State whether this ramp meets the guideline, and give a reason.

options.feedback: Correct. The calculated angle is compared with the limit, and 8.9° is below 10°, so the ramp meets the guideline.
Compare the two numbers again: 8.9 is smaller than 10, so the ramp is inside the limit.

options.text: Yes, because the ramp is 5.8 m long
options.feedback: The guideline is about the angle, not the length. The comparison has to use the angle from part (a).
Part (a) gives the angle, and the guideline gives the limit, which is everything the comparison needs.

hints: Compare your angle from part (a) with the limit.
A decision question needs the comparison written down, not just the word.
parts.workedSolution: The ramp makes an angle of $8.9°$ with the horizontal, and $8.9 < 10$, so the ramp does meet the guideline.

parts.stem:
Órla is holding a drone on a taut cable 40 m long. The cable makes an angle of 38° with the horizontal, and her hand is 120 cm above the ground.

Work out the height of the drone above the ground. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: The cable is the hypotenuse, and the height above her hand is opposite the angle.
The triangle starts at her hand, so add the hand height at the end.
Convert the centimetres to metres before adding.
parts.workedSolution:
The cable is the hypotenuse, so $\sin 38° = \dfrac{h}{40}$ and $h = 40\sin 38° = 24.6265$ m above her hand.

Her hand is 120 cm $= 1.2$ m above the ground, so the drone is $24.6265 + 1.2 = 25.8265$ m up, which is $25.8$ m.

commonErrors.feedback: The 120 has been added as metres. Convert first: 120 cm is 1.2 m, and that is what joins the height from the triangle.
That is the height above her hand only. The triangle sits on her hand, so the hand height belongs in the total.
Cosine gives the horizontal distance, not the height. The height is opposite the angle, so use sine.

figures.alt: A right-angled triangle ABD with the right angle at D. AD is 14 m along the ground, the angle at A is 36 degrees, and BD is the vertical post.

parts.stem:
A vertical post BD stands on level ground. From a point A on the ground, 14 m from the foot D of the post, the angle of elevation of the top B is 36°.

Calculate the height of the post. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: The post is opposite the angle; the ground is adjacent.
Opposite and adjacent means tangent.

commonErrors.feedback: Sine has been used with the ground as if it were the hypotenuse. The two sides here are opposite and adjacent, so the ratio is tangent.
Tangent is the right ratio, so that mark stands. The unknown is on the top of the fraction, so it is found by multiplying by the tangent, not dividing by it.

parts.stem:
C is a point on the ground on the other side of the post from A, with DC $= 8$ m.

Calculate the angle of elevation from C up to B. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: tan C = BD / 8 with the unrounded BD

scheme.examinerNote: Carrying the rounded BD gives a different final decimal place; the scheme rewards the full value

hints: The post is the same height in both triangles.
Use the unrounded value of BD from part (a).
Opposite over adjacent again, then the inverse tangent.
parts.workedSolution: Using the full value $BD = 10.17160$ m, $\tan C = \dfrac{10.17160}{8} = 1.2714$, so $C = 51.8148°$, which is $51.8°$.

commonErrors.feedback: The rounded 10.2 m was carried into the second triangle, and the answer drifts. Keep the full display between steps: the Summer 2025 report put the lost accuracy mark down to exactly this.
The two sides are the wrong way up: the post is opposite the angle at C, and DC is adjacent to it.

findTheMistake.stem: A ramp 11.5 m long makes an angle of 43° with the horizontal ground. Ryan was asked for the horizontal distance the ramp covers. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is a correct labelling. Line 2 chooses sine, which pairs the hypotenuse with the side opposite the angle — that is the height the ramp rises. The horizontal distance lies next to the 43° angle, so it is the adjacent side and the ratio is cosine.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark stands for a correct method structure. The habit that prevents it is labelling the sides on the diagram — O, A and H — before choosing a ratio. November 2025 M3 Q24 turned on this: cosine was needed, and the report says many assumed a different side was wanted and used tangent instead.

findTheMistake.stem: A post stands vertically at D. From A, 9 m away, the angle of elevation of the top is 28°. C is 6 m from D on the other side. Beth was asked for the angle of elevation of the top from C. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The height is found correctly in line 1 and earns its marks. Line 2 rounds it to 1 decimal place and that rounded value is then used in the second triangle, so the final angle drifts: the full value gives $38.6°$, not $38.7°$.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three of the four marks stand; only the accuracy mark is lost. Use the calculator's answer key or memory to carry the exact value into the next line, and round once at the very end. Summer 2025 M4 Q16 lost the same mark for the same reason.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor stands 52 m from a tower on level ground. His eyes are 145 cm above the ground and the angle of elevation of the top is 29°. He was asked for the height of the tower. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The trigonometry is right and both method marks stand. Line 3 adds 145 as though it were metres, which makes the tower over a hundred metres tall. The eye height is 145 cm, and 145 cm $= 1.45$ m.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks stand for the trigonometry. Before adding two lengths, check that they are in the same unit, and ask whether the answer is sensible for a tower. Summer 2023 M4 Q12 recorded a common wrong answer that came from exactly this, and M3 Q23 the same year lost marks to a height in centimetres.

prompts.prompt: Write out SOH CAH TOA in full.
prompts.answer: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse; cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse; tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.

prompts.prompt: How do you label a right-angled triangle before choosing a ratio?
prompts.answer: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Then, from the angle you are using, the side facing it is the opposite and the side beside it is the adjacent.

prompts.prompt: Is SOH CAH TOA on the CCEA formula sheet?
prompts.answer: No. The sheet gives the sine rule, the cosine rule and (1/2)ab sin C, which are for triangles without a right angle. The three ratios must be known.

prompts.prompt: cos 40° = 12 ÷ h. How do you find h?
prompts.answer: Multiply both sides by h, then divide by cos 40°: h = 12 ÷ cos 40°. When the unknown is underneath, the final step is a division.

prompts.prompt: Two sides are known and you want the angle. What do you do?
prompts.answer: Write the ratio those two sides give, then apply the inverse: sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹. The ratio on its own is not the angle.

prompts.prompt: What is an angle of elevation, and what is an angle of depression?
prompts.answer: Both are measured from the horizontal. Elevation is the angle you look up through; depression is the angle you look down through.

prompts.prompt: An angle of depression from a cliff top: which angle in the triangle is it equal to?
prompts.answer: The angle of elevation from the object at the bottom, because the two horizontal lines are parallel and these are alternate angles.

prompts.prompt: Why must you not round a side before using it in a second triangle?
prompts.answer: The error carries into the next calculation and moves the final answer, which costs the accuracy mark. Keep the full calculator value and round once at the end.

prompts.prompt: An isosceles triangle has no right angle. How do you use trigonometry on it?
prompts.answer: Drop a perpendicular from the apex to the base. That makes two right-angled triangles, each with half the base, and it gives half the angle at the apex, so double it at the end.

prompts.prompt: A height in centimetres has to be added to a length in metres. What comes first?
prompts.answer: Convert: divide the centimetres by 100. Adding without converting is a wrong answer the examiners have traced more than once.

prompts.prompt: A ladder 4.6 m long leans at 71° to the ground. How far is its foot from the wall?
prompts.answer: 1.5 m. The ground is adjacent to the angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse, so the distance is 4.6 × cos 71° = 1.4977 m.

findings.asked: Find a side with sine, then add a person's height to get a total height.
findings.wentWrong: Most got the side; the common wrong final answer (89.02) came from adding 85 cm as if it were 85 m.
findings.rule: Convert to the same unit before adding.

findings.asked: Height of a kite plus the height of the holder.
findings.wentWrong: Trigonometry recognised, but the holder's height was forgotten or not converted to metres, and early rounding spoiled answers.
findings.rule: Hold rounding until the last step of a multi-step problem.

findings.asked: A symmetrical (isosceles) triangle that must be halved.
findings.wentWrong: Weaker candidates used the full base (1.4 m) instead of half (0.7 m) and scored zero; most used sine correctly once halved; the cosine rule also worked.
findings.rule: Drop the perpendicular to make a right angle, and halve the base.

findings.asked: Multi-step: Pythagoras, an angle, then tan for another side, then a sum.
findings.wentWrong: About 40% full marks. Some found the first side and could not choose a ratio next; quite a few stopped after three marks.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Found AD by Pythagoras, angle ABD, used the right angle to get DBC, tan for DC, then added.
findings.rule: In a chain, write what each triangle gives you before moving to the next.

findings.asked: Angle a ladder makes with the ground.
findings.wentWrong: Some worked with the angle at the wall; weaker candidates saw two sides and used Pythagoras for a third instead of finding an angle.
findings.rule: An angle question needs an inverse trig ratio, not Pythagoras.

findings.asked: A two-triangle problem: sine to find a shared side, then cosine.
findings.wentWrong: Most knew the sequence; rounding within the calculation lost the accuracy mark; weaker candidates used Pythagoras on unrelated sides or left it blank.
findings.rule: Carry the unrounded shared side into the second triangle.

findings.wentWrong: Under a fifth got all three marks: cos was identified but not rearranged; many assumed a different side was wanted and used tan.
findings.rule: Label H, O, A from the given angle and rearrange before substituting.

findings.asked: Trigonometry used twice across two triangles.
findings.wentWrong: Well answered; those who lost everything used the wrong angle or ratio; some got four marks then could not find the final angle or forgot to round to 1 d.p.

insight.ruleToRemember: Label the triangle from the angle you have, write the ratio, rearrange before substituting, carry full accuracy between steps, and convert units before adding lengths.
insight.aStarSignal: A two- or three-triangle chain where the shared side is carried unrounded and the right ratio is chosen each time.
